title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). The experiment used a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine). A single shared initial candidate was generated per task by gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120). A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks and triggered ≤1 repair only when validator.violation_count>0. Outcomes: baseline success = 120/120 (1.00); guarded success = 120/120 (1.00). Contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Validator traces show repair_applied=false for all guarded episodes. We incorporate clarifications requested during peer review (shared-generation semantics, repair-trigger logic, and artifact-grounded explanation of statistical degeneracy) and expand methodology, execution accounting, representative diagnostics, reproducibility guidance, and limitations grounded in archived artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can produce human-readable network configuration commands from natural-language intent, promising faster NetOps workflows. However, plausible-looking commands may nonetheless violate workflow constraints (for example, requiring a shutdown step before changing MTU or making unsafe uplink switchover sequences), produce regressions, or break invariants that a live network depends on. Prior proposals therefore recommend integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers into LLM-driven NetOps pipelines so that generated candidates are checked and, when necessary, repaired before enactment. Evaluating such guarded pipelines requires closed-loop executable tests that expose semantic/network-level failures beyond token- or syntax-level correctness. We studied whether adding an executable emulator validator and a single-step repair mechanism reduces emulator-observed semantic failures relative to an LLM-only suggestion workflow under a tightly scoped, preregistered paired design.

Our confirmatory research question (preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) asked: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair effects from generation variance we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: the same generation was presented to both conditions for each task. This isolates the marginal effect of validation/repair on identical generator outputs. The present paper reports the preregistered design, exact execution accounting, confirmatory statistical results, per-topology counts, representative validator traces, and an artifact-grounded interpretation of a degenerate ceiling outcome observed in the run.
sections.related_work:
Recent benchmarks and tool-papers emphasize that evaluation limited to generated-text correctness can miss operational failure modes. Several contemporary efforts produce executable benchmarks, digital twins, or verification layers to assess closed-loop outcomes for LLM-driven NetOps: NetConfArena and similar executable testbeds evaluate agentic behavior in emulation, while other work shows that generate→validate→repair architectures reduce semantic errors in constrained scenarios. Surveys and tool papers also repeatedly propose guardrails — e.g., veto layers, canary deployments, and model→formal-model translation patterns — as practical safety measures for agentic NetOps.

Where prior studies aggregate end-to-end systems across models and tool stacks, our experiment takes a complementary, narrowly scoped approach: it holds the generator fixed and asks whether the validator/repair stage provides incremental safety benefits for identical generated candidates. This isolates an important mechanism often conflated in multi-component evaluations. Our design and findings should therefore be interpreted in the methodological context of paired, shared-generation tests rather than as an assertion about multi-model or production-wide generality.

The literature also documents important evidence gaps that motivated our preregistered exploratory agenda: (1) the scarcity of large, production-rooted corpora of misconfiguration incidents with verifiable ground truth; (2) limited cross-model comparisons under identical executable harnesses; and (3) under-explored methods for providing calibrated, actionable uncertainty estimates on structured configuration outputs. These gaps guided our emphasis on deterministic, artifact-rich archival practices so that future cross-run comparisons can reuse the same task bank, validator, and manifests.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) and archived before execution. The preregistration specified a paired-binary design with exactly N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks, deterministically assigned into three topology classes (edge, core, leaf–spine) with 40 tasks each. Each task produced a single shared initial candidate generated by gpt-5-mini (requested_model: "gpt-5-mini") and used by both conditions. Per the preregistration, a guarded repair could be invoked at most once and only when the deterministic emulator validator reported validator.violation_count>0.

Generation stage: All shared initial candidates were produced by the declared hosted model (gpt-5-mini) under the archived model configuration (execution/model_configuration.json). The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 120; planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240. The pairing parameter independent_condition_generation=false in the preregistration enforced identical generator outputs across conditions to isolate validator/repair effects. The shared-generation stage was recorded for every task (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 120).

Validator and repair mechanism: The guarded pipeline integrated a deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, validator_version = 5.0). This validator executed intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks (examples encoded in the task payloads: must_be_down_for_fields, make-before-break patterns, final_group_constraints). The validator implemented a full_intent_constraint_validation scoring rule and produced structured validator_trace artifacts per episode containing validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, and violation_count. The preregistered repair policy required repair_applied only when violation_count>0; the repair budget was ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode. Repair prompts and repair_provider_trace artifacts would be archived when used; none were recorded because no violations occurred.

Task generation and difficulty strata: The task bank is a deterministic synthetic corpus generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest entry includes constraints, an explicit required_sequence describing the correct ordering of field changes (for example, shut→mtu→vlan→up), an initial_state, and expected_final_state. Tasks were labeled with difficulty level (medium/hard/very_hard) and encoded dependency_rule_count and required_command_count; these metadata permit stratified reanalysis.

Primary estimand and statistical plan: The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (the per-pair reduction in emulator-observed semantic-failure probability). The prespecified confirmatory test was the exact two-sided McNemar. Complementary inferential reporting included the paired-difference estimate and a bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples and bootstrap_seed = 1729 (these bootstrap parameters were recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The preregistration specified a complete-pair primary analysis; technical/instrumentation failures would be excluded and logged, with sensitivity analyses treating excluded items as failures.

Instrumentation and contamination controls: The execution harness recorded provider-call audit logs and enforced deterministic emulator-state reset between tasks (container image checks and deterministic seeds). Contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection, cross-condition cache-key reuse) were applied and logged; none triggered exclusions. All raw provider traces, responses, and scorer JSONs were archived along with an execution manifest for post-hoc verification.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes: The run completed the planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 240) and produced one shared initial generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline = 120 successes, 0 failures and guarded = 120 successes, 0 failures (success rates = 1.0 for both conditions). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. analysis/missingness_summary.csv indicates complete_pairs = 120 and zero technical/instrumentation exclusions.

Confirmatory statistics: With zero discordant pairs the exact two-sided McNemar p-value equals 1.0. The paired-difference estimate is 0.00. The preregistered bootstrap percentile confidence interval computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) returned [0.00, 0.00]; the CI is degenerate because resampling an empirical table with no discordant pairs reproduces identical paired outcomes across resamples. The analysis/analysis_log.jsonl records the bootstrap parameters and the completed paired analysis event.

Per-topology counts and representative diagnostics: Tasks were deterministically assigned 40 per topology class. Per-topology aggregated success counts from archived artifacts are:
- Edge (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Core (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Leaf–spine (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
These per-topology summaries are supported by execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries and the scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/.

Representative validator traces: Representative scoring JSONs included in the archive (for example, execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json and -baseline.json) show normalized_response matching normalized_reference_answer, parsed_command_count equal to required_command_count, validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, and validator_trace.repair_applied = false. The artifact examples demonstrate the validator's structured output fields (validation_before and validation_after difficulties, touched_field counts, and violation lists), which can be used to reconstruct the semantic-check logic.

Repair activity: The preregistered guarded repair policy was conditional on validator.violation_count>0. Because violation_count = 0 for every guarded episode, repair_applied = false across the archive, and no repair_provider_trace artifacts exist. Consequently, preregistered secondary endpoints—proportion of tasks requiring repair and mean repair calls per successful task—are vacuous for this run.

Contamination, missingness, and deterministic reconciliation: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (no flags). Deterministic reconciliation artifacts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirm consistent episode accounting (n_11=120, provider_call_audit showing hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, no cache hits). No preregistered deviations or exclusions were logged.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling/null outcome: The run's shared-generation design intentionally removed generation variance so that any difference between conditions would arise solely from the validator/repair stage operating on identical candidates. In this experiment the shared initial candidates produced by gpt-5-mini all satisfied the deterministic emulator validator's encoded intent constraints and workflow policies, producing a concordant-success ceiling (n_11=120). Under these conditions the guarded pipeline could not exercise repair behavior and therefore could not reduce semantic failures relative to baseline. The observed exact McNemar p=1.0 and bootstrap CI=[0.00,0.00] are statistical manifestations of this ceiling.

Methodological implications: The paired shared-generation design answers a precise mechanistic question — whether a validator/repair stage can improve outcomes for identical generator outputs — and the answer in this task bank and under the archived generator/prompting configuration is "no effect" because the generator produced only valid candidates. However, this narrow null result should not be extrapolated to imply that guarded pipelines are unnecessary in broader settings. In practice, generator variance, adversarial inputs, prompt perturbations, alternative model families, or production heterogeneity may produce invalid candidates for which a validator/repair subsystem could be decisive.

Design recommendations for future work: To measure practical repair utility, confirmatory tests should allow independent per-condition generation so that the guard can act on generator errors produced under realistic prompting variability. Additional recommendations include expanding the repair budget to multiple repair iterations, testing multiple generator models and prompt perturbation schemes, and incorporating multi-vendor behavioral models in the validator. The archived task_manifest includes difficulty metadata (dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, and difficulty level) that supports stratified future comparisons across workload classes.

External and construct validity concerns: The deterministic emulator validator operationalizes semantic correctness using encoded workflow policies derived from the task payloads; this reproducible approach trades realism for determinism. The synthetic task corpus simplifies vendor heterogeneity, telemetry availability, and partial observability that characterize production networks. Consequently, external validity to live multi-vendor infrastructures is limited. The preregistered power assumptions (target absolute reduction = 0.15) were not met because the baseline succeeded on the entire curated task set, making the primary test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.

Practical operational implications: The archival artifacts document how a reproducible validator can be integrated and audited: validator traces show structured fields that can be used to build operator-facing explanations (what rule passed/failed, which fields were touched, and why a repair was or was not applied). Even when the validator is unused (as here), maintaining deterministic validator outputs and recorded decision traces supports operator auditability and post-hoc incident analysis. The archived provider-call audit and deterministic reconciliations demonstrate how to instrument runs for accountable operation.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing n_11=120 (baseline and guarded successes) and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed=1729). The result documents a ceiling effect on this curated synthetic task bank and clarifies that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. We supply comprehensive archived artifacts (model configuration, task manifest, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts) so that future studies can (1) relax shared-generation constraints, (2) test multiple models and prompt perturbations, and (3) evaluate repair budgets and validator fidelity against more production-rooted corpora. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we demonstrate how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and we show how deterministic archival artifacts support reproducible failure analyses even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
